report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: The funders had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish or preparation of the manuscript.
No datasets were generated or analysed during the current study.
Cognitive science has made substantial progress in understanding how minds extend into and are shaped by their material and social environments.

The predictive processing framework (PP), 4E cognition, material engagement theory (MET), and cultural learning research have described cognition as not skin-bounded, context-neutral, or culturally invariant.

Yet there is still much to be said about the developing mind: about how cognition emerges, transforms, and is shaped by its material and cultural embeddings in the early stages of childhood and adolescence.

This paper argues that some resources for a richer account have been available for over a century, in the work of a scientist who has been consistently present in educational discourse and consistently absent from the history of science.
That scientist is Maria Montessori.

Conceived at the beginning of the twentieth century, her method is organised around the idea that development and learning are embodied and enacted processes, in which the sensorimotor system and cognition are intertwined, and in which knowledge, concepts, and higher cognitive abilities emerge dynamically from the interaction between children's autonomous exploration and their material embeddings (Di Paolo et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Conceived at the beginning of the twentieth century, her method is organised around the idea that development and learning are embodied and enacted processes, in which the sensorimotor system and cognition are intertwined, and in which knowledge, concepts, and higher cognitive abilities emerge dynamically from the interaction between children's autonomous exploration and their material embeddings <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Di Paolo et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Teaching happens indirectly, through the design and organisation of what Montessori called the "prepared environment" (l'ambiente preparato) an immersive ecology of purposely designed educational objects, organised in hierarchical complexity and presented by teachers at developmentally appropriate moments.

Not a pedagogical convenience, the prepared environment is an engineered site where the mechanisms linking individual development, designed material culture, and cultural context are made explicit and tractable.
1 A note on sources and translations: Throughout this paper, we draw on Montessori's published corpus in both Italian and English.
Two conventions require explanation.

First, we do not provide specific citations when referring to ideas or claims that Montessori articulates repeatedly and consistently across her corpus, such as her insistence on the centrality of observation, the role of the prepared environment, or the importance of sensitive periods.
Where a claim is specific to a particular text or passage, full citations are provided as usual.
Second, where discrepancies exist between the Italian and English versions of Montessori's texts, whether in meaning, theoretical precision, or tone, we give priority to the Italian.
There are two reasons for this.

One of the authors is an Italian native speaker, educated in history of science, philosophy, and philosophy of biology and natural sciences at La Sapienza, University of Rome, and has additionally studied palaeoanthropology in the very department founded by Giuseppe Sergi, a disciplinary and institutional continuity that informs the reading of both Sergi's and Montessori's texts offered here.
More importantly, the Italian versions of Montessori's major works, independently of their complex publication histories, were always revised by Montessori herself in her preferred language.
The available English translations, while serviceable, frequently modify phrasing to enhance fluency at the cost of theoretical precision, a problem we document in detail in Section 3.
The Italian text should therefore be regarded as authoritative wherever the two diverge.
The scientist of the developing mind: formation and framework Montessori is remembered as the founder of a global educational movement.

She was trained as something considerably more specific: a scientist of the developing mind, formed at the intersection of biological anthropology, experimental psychology, comparative anatomy, psychiatry, and the nascent behavioural sciences of late nineteenth-century Rome.
Understanding what she built requires understanding where she came from, not biographically but intellectually.
Her formation was not incidental to her method.
It was its foundation.

Montessori began her university studies at the Faculty of Natural Sciences at La Sapienza in Rome in 1890, attending classes in zoology and comparative anatomy before transferring to the Faculty of Medicine, where she earned her degree in psychiatry (Foschi, 2012; Kramer, 1988; Matellicani, 2007).
text.formatted: Montessori began her university studies at the Faculty of Natural Sciences at La Sapienza in Rome in 1890, attending classes in zoology and comparative anatomy before transferring to the Faculty of Medicine, where she earned her degree in psychiatry <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Foschi, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Kramer, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Matellicani, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: She subsequently returned to La Sapienza for a second degree in philosophy, completed between 1904 and 1907 at the faculty that today houses philosophy and education.
This trajectory, from natural sciences, to medicine, psychiatry, and eventually philosophy, is not the curriculum of an educator.
Rather, of someone attempting to understand the human mind from a multidisciplinary perspective.

Her formation unfolded within the specific intellectual environment of late nineteenth-century Rome, shaped above all by two figures with whom Montessori had sustained and formative relationships: the anthropologist Giuseppe Sergi and the experimental psychologist Sante De Sanctis.

While Montessori started working as a psychiatrist and as a doctorhttps://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/RiQJ+5bAL+XPDX+OKKk and was engaged with social battles for the welfare of children and women (Babini, 2023; Foschi, 2012; Montessori, 1898a Montessori, , 1898b)) , she came into contact with the anthropologist Giuseppe Sergi (1841 Sergi ( -1936)).

text.text: Sergi was a physical and biological anthropologist, a strenuous defender of evolutionary theory in an Italian academic environment increasingly drawn toward idealism, and a public intellectual engaged with the social implications of science (Cerro, 2017; Foschi, 2012; Pesci, 2022a)  5 .

text.text: His influence on Montessori was enormous: she consistently referred to him as "il maestro", and provided the fundamental framework of her analysis.

Central to understanding that influence is a little pamphlet published by Sergi in 1884 (Sergihttps://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/N2Cs 1884) , titled "Antropologia Biologica" [Biological Anthropology], largely unknown to international scholarship and unmentioned even in most Italian accounts of the Montessori-Sergi relationship (Cerro, 2017; Matellicani, brain is "the organ of the mind" and that anthropology cannot exclude the study of psychical functions reflects a specific philosophical position: a naturalistic monism that refused the separation of the physical and the mental while rejecting both crude materialism and spiritualism.

text.text: This position placed him within a tradition running from Helmholtz's physiological psychology through to contemporary cognitive science, and it is the philosophical foundation that Montessori inherited along with the methodological programme.
Sergi was not, in other words, simply a source of empirical methods and evolutionary concepts.
He gave Montessori a philosophy of mind, one in which the brain, behaviour, and environment are irreducibly connected, that underlies everything she subsequently built.

text.text: In this text, Sergi drafted the guidelines for what he called a "living science"a science in which both the structures and the functions of human organisms must be taken into account.

Anthropology, he argued, is "the most vast of the sciences" precisely because it must absorb knowledge from psychology, sociology, ethnology, medicine, and what we would today call ethology or animal behaviour (Sergi, 1884) https://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/N2Cs 3).

text.text: Most importantly for our purposes, Sergi insisted that the brain is "the organ of the mind" and that it would be "strange" if anthropology excluded the study of its psychical functions (Ibid.: 3-4).

The comparison he drew with ethological studies is striking in its contemporary resonance: just as zoology had moved beyond mere classification toward the observation of animal behaviour in relationship to the physical environment, anthropology needed to enter "a new phase of research and observations" in which human beings are studied in all their manifestations within "the composite environment in which the man lives and multiplies" (Ibid.: 5; 8).
This is recognisably a proto-cognitive science programme.

Sergi was proposing an integrated study of structure and function, brain and behaviour, individual and environment, that anticipates the agenda of contemporary cognitive science with remarkable precision [see, e.g. (Clark, 2004 (Clark, , 2016;; Clark & Chalmers, 1998; Newen et al., 2018; Varela et al., 2018) https://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/IKP8+g7s2+9o8J+AbA0+248Z.

text.text: He went further, identifying three environments within which human existence unfolds -physical, organic, and social -and arguing that anthropological phenomena of both biological and psychical nature are produced within all three simultaneously (Ibid.: 7-8).
The organism, he wrote, "modifies and adapts, or tries to adapt to the alive and continuously acting forces of external nature" (Ibid.: 6).
This ecosystemic conception of the human organism is precisely the framework that Montessori would elaborate into a theory of cognitive development in the prepared environment and its materials.
Sergi also transmitted to Montessori a specifically evolutionary and biological mindset that shaped her understanding of development in ways that have been consistently underestimated.

His "frank Darwinian evolutionism," as Pesci [(https://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/8XCy 24)] characterises it, gave Montessori the conceptual tools to think about childhood as a period of biological and cognitive formation rather than simply a stage of preparation for adult life.
text.formatted: His "frank Darwinian evolutionism," as Pesci [(<ref type="url" target="https://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/8XCy">Pesci, 2022a):</ref> 24)] characterises it, gave Montessori the conceptual tools to think about childhood as a period of biological and cognitive formation rather than simply a stage of preparation for adult life.

text.text: Within this biological framework, the concept of 'variation' (i.e., any difference among a population, genetic or phenotypic) gave Montessori the conceptual tools for understanding and accounting for inter-individual differences in children's development.
Each child, in Montessori's view, is considered a variation, a specific phenotype whose cognitive development unfolds through interaction with an individual environment.

This is the reason why, even today, in Montessori schools children with diverse learning styles and neurodivergent profiles are more easily accommodated and welcomed (Foster, 2025; Koifman, 2025 https://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/gSbX+HoZN.
text.formatted: This is the reason why, even today, in Montessori schools children with diverse learning styles and neurodivergent profiles are more easily accommodated and welcomed <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Foster, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Koifman, 2025</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/gSbX+HoZN">)</ref>.

text.text: Sergi's influence extended to the methodology of observation, which became essential to her programme (Foschi, 2012).
text.formatted: Sergi's influence extended to the methodology of observation, which became essential to her programme <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Foschi, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: He insisted that the study of human beings required not only experimental methods but sustained anthropological observation: the patient, systematic recording of behaviour in naturalistic conditions.
This methodological commitment, which Montessori absorbed directly, became one of the most distinctive features of her approach and one of the most misunderstood.
American psychologists like Dewey and his followers read her insistence on observation as a rejection of experimental science (Kilpatrick, 1914; Thayer-Bacon, 2012).
text.formatted: American psychologists like Dewey and his followers read her insistence on observation as a rejection of experimental science <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Kilpatrick, 1914;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b135">Thayer-Bacon, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: It was in fact a different and in some respects more sophisticated conception of what experimental science required, one that anticipated the later turn in cognitive science toward naturalistic and ecological methods, including the 4E account of cognition (Chemero, 2013; Fabry, 2025; Rietveld & Kiverstein, 2014).
text.formatted: It was in fact a different and in some respects more sophisticated conception of what experimental science required, one that anticipated the later turn in cognitive science toward naturalistic and ecological methods, including the 4E account of cognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Chemero, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Fabry, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b125">Rietveld & Kiverstein, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Sergi was also the figure who introduced Montessori to the overlap between anthropological observation and education.

His own writings on pedagogy, including Educazione ed istruzione (1892) [Education and Instruction] and L'educazione del carattere (1893) [The Education of the Character], anticipate many of the themes Montessori would develop: a school without punishments and 'military' discipline; the importance of the physical environment for learning; the introduction of experimental sciences into educational settings; and the role of attention, imitation, and social interaction in cognitive development (Pesci, 2002).

text.text: He even proposed that a "naturalist psychologist", that is, someone trained in biological anthropology and experimental psychology simultaneously, should be present in schools as an observer of children's behaviour.
It is difficult not to read this as a description of exactly what Montessori would become.

The second formative relationship was with Sante De Sanctis, who supervised Montessori's thesis in psychiatry, collaborated with her at the Orthophrenic Hospital, and later taught her psychology at the Faculty of Philosophy (Matellicani, 2007; Pesci, 2002).

text.text: For the academic year 1903-1904, Montessori attended De Sanctis's lessons three times a week.
The intellectual debt is traceable and specific.

De Sanctis's primary scientific interests during the period of his closest contact with Montessori covered attention and its disorders, voluntary attention investigated experimentally, the psychophysiology of attention in typical and psychopathological subjects, the scientific method, dreams and emotions, and the anatomical, physiological, and biological foundations of psychopathology (Matellicani, 2007).

text.text: Attention, in particular, is central to Montessori's entire pedagogical and theoretical framework: the concept of 'concentration', the design of materials to capture and sustain attention, the observation of attentional patterns as the primary data of her experimental method (https://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/xC0h+8ngT+rpd0. Lillard, 2011; Rathunde, 2001; Sobe, 2004).

text.text: De Sanctis gave her the theoretical framework for understanding attention as a cognitive function with developmental stages, and the experimental tools for studying it.
His theory of attention is worth examining briefly because of its direct relevance to Montessori's method.

De Sanctis distinguished between the concentrative function of attention (i.e., its capacity to fix on a single object) and its distributive function (i.e., its capacity to coordinate multiple objects simultaneously) (https://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/1HP1) see also: (Cimino & Lombardo, 2004).
text.formatted: De Sanctis distinguished between the concentrative function of attention (i.e., its capacity to fix on a single object) and its distributive function (i.e., its capacity to coordinate multiple objects simultaneously) (<ref type="url" target="https://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/1HP1">De Sanctis, 1896</ref>) see also: <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Cimino & Lombardo, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: He observed that in children, distributive attention is not yet developed, while strong concentrative attention (fixation on a task or object) is characteristically present.
Development consists in the gradual elaboration of distributive from concentrative attention, through both growth and exercise.
This developmental account maps directly onto Montessori's observation that children in the prepared environment characteristically enter states of deep concentration.
She called them "polarisation of attention", and considered them the primary mechanism of cognitive development (Montessori, 2014).
text.formatted: She called them "polarisation of attention", and considered them the primary mechanism of cognitive development <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Montessori, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The prepared environment, with its carefully designed materials and its freedom from interruption, is structured precisely to enable and extend this concentrative state.

De Sanctis also transmitted to Montessori a vision of pedagogy as a science that requires both experimental psychology and biological anthropology, a vision that maps exactly onto the same interdisciplinary programme that Sergi had outlined.

In fact, together with Sergi, De Sanctis was the founder of the Rivista quindicinale di Psicologia, Psichiatria, Neuropatologia [Fortnightly Journal of Author's Manuscript Submitted to History of Psychology Psychology, Psychiatry, and Neuropathology], which pursued and diffused a multidisciplinary approach to cognition and the mind.

Accordingly, De Sanctis's lectures on pedagogical psychology, which Montessori attended, described education as the attempt to follow the development of human capacities through "observations and deductions obtained through facts" that are always both physiological and psychological, individual and social (De Sanctis, 1913; in Pesci, 2002).

text.text: His insistence that pedagogy does not deal with the abstract student but with a "real individual" -"not schemata are needed, but the knowledge of living things; not theories, but experiences" (De Sanctis, 1922; in Pesci, 2002: 190-191)anticipates almost exactly Montessori's own methodological commitments.

James, whose minor works De Sanctis had translated and used in his lectures as "an alternative to dry positivism, without yielding to the temptations of spiritualistic and anti-positivistic currents" (https://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/8XCy 25-26).

text.text: James's pragmatist and functionalist psychology, and insistence on the continuity of mind and action, on habit as the flywheel of behaviour, on the stream of consciousness as an active and selective rather than passive and receptive process, reinforced the framework Montessori was absorbing from Sergi and De Sanctis and added a specifically functionalist dimension that would later connect her work with what today counts as 4E cognition: the family of accounts holding that cognition is embodied, embedded, enacted, and extended beyond the boundaries of the brain and into the body, the environment, and the artefacts with which organisms interact (Chemero, 2013; Newen et al., 2018; Varela et al., 2018).

text.text: Even from this brief analysis of only some elements of Montessori's formation -the bio-anthropological training under Sergi, and the immersion in De Sanctis's experimental psychology of attention -an interest in the mind and its cognitive functions is already visible.
This interest would be developed, both theoretically and practically in her method, along three dimensions: the individual, the material, and the socio-cultural.
Following De Sanctis's insistence on the "real individual" as the proper subject of pedagogy, Montessori directed her attention not to the child but to each child: each one different from the others.
This difference, given her biological formation, is to be read in an evolutionary sense: each child is a variation shaped by its particular genotype and its particular developmental history.
Inter-individual differences in learning are not problems to be corrected but data to be observed and taken into account.
The educational environment must accommodate and reveal these differences, not erase them (https://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/2efl+kXay. Frierson, 2018; Politi, 2023).
text.formatted: The educational environment must accommodate and reveal these differences, not erase them (<ref type="url" target="https://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/2efl+kXay">P</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Frierson, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b117">Politi, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The second is the material dimension.

Cognitive development does not happen in an abstract space but through concrete engagement with a material world of objects, spaces, tools, and artefacts, exactly what MET (Malafouris, 2013) identifies as the constitutive role of physical things in cognitive processes.
text.formatted: Cognitive development does not happen in an abstract space but through concrete engagement with a material world of objects, spaces, tools, and artefacts, exactly what MET <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Malafouris, 2013)</ref> identifies as the constitutive role of physical things in cognitive processes.

text.text: The mind, in Montessori's account, is formed in and through its engagement with the material world.

The educational materials she designed are not aids to a process that happens independently of them: they are essential to the process (https://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/R3Q6+GgLc. Frierson & Di Paolo, 2025; A. Lillard, 2008).

text.text: The third is the social and cultural dimension.

The child develops within a cultural environment that is not merely a context but a constitutive condition of cognitive development -exactly what cultural learning Author's Manuscript Submitted to History of Psychology research identifies as the irreducibly social character of human cognitive formation (Heyes, 2018; Tomasello, 2009).

text.text: Language, social norms, cultural practices, and artefacts are absorbed by the developing mind not as external additions to a pre-formed cognitive system but as the medium through which the cognitive system is formed (https://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/YlY8.
text.formatted: Language, social norms, cultural practices, and artefacts are absorbed by the developing mind not as external additions to a pre-formed cognitive system but as the medium through which the cognitive system is formed (<ref type="url" target="https://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/YlY8">Sterelny, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Montessori's concept of the mente assorbente, i.e. the capacity proper of the young child to take in and internalise the cultural environment, is a theoretical claim about the relationship between mind and culture, not merely a metaphor.
These three dimensions -individual, material, cultural -are irreducible and simultaneous.
No adequate account of cognitive development can proceed by holding any one of them constant while varying the others.

This is the framework that the misreading (see Section 3) has consistently failed to see, reading the individual dimension as a philosophy of child-centred education, the material dimension as a collection of didactic toys, and the cultural dimension as a vague commitment to holistic development.

It is also, as we shall argue in the following section, the framework that the prepared environment was designed to make explicit and tractable, which is why it functions as a model system for cognitive science rather than merely as a successful educational method.
The prepared environment [ambiente preparato] is perhaps the central contribution of Montessori's method, at once theoretical and practical.
It is the solution to a practical problem that also constitutes a theoretical claim, because Montessori found herself doing two things at once.

On the theoretical side, her formation in biological anthropology, comparative anatomy, and experimental psychology had given her an understanding of the environment not as the backdrop of development but as the material medium necessary to it -and so she conceived the classroom as the place where "optimal development" could naturally unfold (Catherine et al., 2020; Foschi, 2012; Marshall, 2017; Montessori, 2025; Rathunde, 2023).

text.text: On the practical side, she was effectively in the business of opening schools: real institutions with real obligations to real families and to society as a whole, which meant ensuring that children learned to read, write, and calculate (Caracchini, 2019; Fresco, 2018; Giovetti, 2014; Regni, 2007).

text.text: The prepared environment, then, had to satisfy both demands at once: it had to respect and leverage the actual mechanisms of cognitive development, while reliably producing specific cognitive outcomes.
The solution was to recognise that these demands were not in tension.
The most effective way to ensure children learn to read, write, and calculate is, in fact, to create an environment that reflects how developing minds actually work.
Children in traditional schools, Montessori argued, are "suffocated" in their natural expressions (Montessori, 1909) https://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/ci5D15) 6 .

The difference is significant: "soffocati" carries the sense of suppression, of something that cannot express itself at all, rather than merely something held back.

The English version flattens a vivid and theoretically loaded term into a much milder one, losing precisely the force of Montessori's claim about what traditional schooling does to the child's natural cognitive development.

text.text: On this account, the brain is not a passive receiver of sensory information but an active prediction machine: it continuously generates expectations about the causes of incoming sensory signals and updates those expectations when they are not met, driving both perception and action.

Learning, in this view, is not the accumulation of facts but the progressive refinement of a model of the world through cycles of prediction and error correction (Friston et al., 2016 (Friston et al., , 2021)).
text.formatted: Learning, in this view, is not the accumulation of facts but the progressive refinement of a model of the world through cycles of prediction and error correction <ref type="bibr">(Friston et al., 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Friston et al., , 2021))</ref>.

text.text: The developing mind is always actively engaged with its environment, not waiting to receive knowledge but reaching out to sample, predict, and revise.

Read through this lens, the prepared environment becomes not a neutral container for learning activities but a deliberately structured cognitive environment, an extension of the predictive mind (Constant et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Read through this lens, the prepared environment becomes not a neutral container for learning activities but a deliberately structured cognitive environment, an extension of the predictive mind <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Constant et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The environment is organised to make the child's active engagement with the world as productive as possible, to ensure that errors are informative rather than discouraging, to support the child's natural drive to predict, explore, understand, and self-regulate, but also to make concrete the teaching of the teachers, who literally not only use the environment, but let the organised environment teach (Ahmadpour & Mujembari, 2015; Denervaud, 2023; Kersna et al., 2025; Kocabaş & Bavlı, 2022).

text.text: It is in this light that the prepared environment can then absolve both functions: upholding optimal development while teaching basic literacy.
It should be taken as an interface situated between the mind and the activity of the children and of the teachers, by design also incorporating a social and community dimension.
The aesthetics of the physical organisation of the Montessori classroom is cognitively motivated.
Everything is children-size -furniture, shelves, storage -so that the material environment is fully accessible to the child's body and perception without adult mediation 7 .

The classroom is divided into clearly organised sections, each dedicated to a specific domain (e.g., mathematics, language, sensorial materials, practical life, cultural subjects) with materials stored in labelled compartments when not in use.
There is always a free, unfurnished space where children can work on the floor, move freely, and observe 7 A fact easily overlooked by contemporary readers deserves mention.
Children-size furniture was not in widespread use before the second half of the nineteenth century.

More broadly, the conceptualisation of childhood as a distinct, protected, and developmentally significant phase of human life was not established before the eighteenth century and was only globally acknowledged in the second half of the nineteenth.

Montessori's insistence on designing an environment scaled to the child's body and calibrated to the child's developmental capacities was not therefore a refinement of existing practice but a historically situated and theoretically motivated intervention, whose radicalism is invisible only in retrospect [e.g., (Lange, 2025) https://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/dM0B.

One of the reasons why Montessori's relationship with the fascist regime ended so abruptly was the regime's insistence on interfering with teacher training programs and selection -beyond the more obvious incompatibility between fascist ideology and the culture of freedom and self-direction characteristic of Montessori schools.
Montessori consistently declared herself apolitical, but she never permitted any government to interfere with the training of her teachers, who were to be educated, not indoctrinated.

As Pesci (2019: 149) puts it: "To any government that interfered, wanting to impose how things should go in her schools -whether the radicals of Catalonia or the fascists in Italy -Montessori would have opposed herself, not necessarily for political reasons, but for pedagogical and educational ones; and not necessarily because Maria could not live in the way they intended to guide their nations, but because only she should determine the way of running her schools" [our translation].

text.text: Submitted to History of Psychology 2.4 Sensitive periods: development as biological fact
The concept of "periodi sensitivi" [sensitive periods] is Montessori's most explicit bridge between her biological formation and her conception of the mind.
Sensitive periods are restricted windows of time in the development of the child during which specific environmental stimuli must occur for the development of particular cognitive capacities.
Outside these windows, the same stimuli have a much reduced effect.

The child who does not encounter written language during its sensitive period for language acquisition will acquire literacy later, with greater difficulty and with a qualitatively different result (Schaefer Zener, 2003).

text.text: But the concept itself had multiple and deeper roots in her formation.
Her studies in zoology and comparative anatomy had introduced her to the concept of developmental phases before and after birth.

Her work with De Sanctis at the Orthophrenic Hospital had given her direct experience of the consequences of missing critical developmental windows in children, particularly those cognitively atypical.
Her reading of Mémoire et Rapport sur Victor de l'Aveyron by Jean Itard had shown her the limits of cognitive development outside the normal cultural environment.

And her sustained cross-cultural observation across several decades had given her empirical evidence that these windows were universal rather than culturally specific (Foschi, 2012; Fresco, 2018; Kramer, 1988; Matellicani, 2007).

text.text: The parallel with Konrad Lorenz's critical periods -which Lorenz formalised in work that earned him the Nobel Prize in 1973, two decades after Montessori's death -has not been fully developed in the literature.
It is worth being precise about the nature of the parallel.
Montessori was not anticipating Lorenz, but was working from the same intellectual tradition: ethology and animal behaviour, and comparative biology.

This passion and knowledge were transmitted to her mainly by Sergi, who wrote in his Anthropologia Biologica (1884) that the study of animal behaviour is very useful and he wishes that anthropology arrives to the very same phase in which ethological studies are: "human morphology is not enough, it is necessary to study the functions and all the series of various and diverse manifestations in the composite environment where the human lives and multiplies" (Ibid.: 5).

Trained with this aim, and in a cultural context in which the idea was spread across nations, she arrived at Lorenz's same theoretical conclusion through independent but convergent routes (Laeng, 2000).

text.text: The developing mind does not weigh all sensory input equally at all developmental stages.
Instead, it weights particular inputs with particular precision at particular moments, making those inputs maximally formative and those moments maximally critical.
The prepared environment is designed to ensure that the right inputs are available with the right precision at the right moments.

In practice, this translates into the introduction of the educational Author's Manuscript Submitted to History of Psychology materials in a specific manner, within a wider developmental window compared to traditional schooling (three to six-year age range instead of just one), and along the teacher's methodological and systematical observation of each child's stage, reactions, and capabilities.
That Montessori has been read only as an educator rather than also as a scientist is not a neutral observation about disciplinary boundaries.
It is the outcome of a specific historical process with identifiable causes.

We identify primarily three, which operated simultaneously and reinforced each other: (a) the transformation of her communicative style under biographical and political pressure; (b) the losses incurred in translation and international reception; and (c) the structural disadvantages she faced as a female scientist in a male-dominated academic environment.
Together they account for a misreading that has persisted for over a century and that has had concrete consequences for the history of cognitive science.
Montessori's earliest publications are unambiguously scientific in character.

Her work in psychiatry, neuroanatomy, and anthropology from the late 1890s was published in technical journals including the Rivista quindicinale di Psicologia, Psichiatria, Neuropatologia [Fortnightly Journal of Psychology, Psychiatry, and Neuropathology] and belongs squarely within the experimental and positivist tradition of late nineteenth-century Italian science (Foschi, 2012; Matellicani, 2007; Trabalzini & Michener-Rutledge, 2023).

The explanation is primarily financial and political, enshrined within a scientific logic that has been consistently overlooked.

text.text: Without entering into a point-by-point rebuttal, which lies beyond the scope of this paper, we want to signal that this reading rests on a failure to situate Montessori's language within the scientific vocabulary of her time and disciplinary context.
L'Antropologia Pedagogica (Montessori, 1911) was the published summary of university lectures Montessori was delivering at La Sapienza: a technical scientific text, not a popular work.

text.text: Its terminology reflects the biological anthropology of late nineteenth-century Italian positivism rather than any ideological commitment.

A reader accustomed to that vocabulary will recognise, for instance, that Montessori uses the word "barbaro" [barbarian] as a "technical" term for isolated or unmixed communities, standard in the biological anthropology of the period.
This is clear from the text itself: "In truth, pure racial types no longer exist, especially where civilisation is most intense.
To speak of racial types, one must go among barbarians, and even this is relative since more or less all the races of the earth have mixed.
And in civilised countries, some pure nucleus can be found in eccentric places, almost escaped from the vortex of civilisation overwhelming the races.

We can contemplate in the history of humanity this merging of races and therefore of morphological characteristics, and the formation of ever more intimate mixtures until the disappearance of the original racial types" (Montessori, 1910: 403-404; our translation).

text.text: Far from advocating racial hierarchy, Montessori is here describing the progressive mixing and disappearance of racial types as a historical fact, a reading entirely consistent with Sergi's evolutionary anthropology.

text.text: Unable to support herself and her projects through institutional channels, she needed her work to be accessible and appealing to a wider audience, who could have allowed her to reach richer sectors of the population, but farther positioned from academia.

Working with and for children, she primarily looked at the nobildonne of Roman and Italian aristocracy, driving her toward a communicative style that was plain, direct, and deliberately stripped of technical apparatus.

Biographers have read this shift as opportunism or diplomacy - Kramer (1988) refers to Montessori's "dual nature" -and it is true that she navigated simultaneously between Catholic nuns, socialists, anthropologists, theosophists, fascists, and pacifists, making her method acceptable across radically different political and cultural contexts (Moretti, 2022).

text.text: This allowed Montessori to expand her method across countries, cultures, and political regimes, thereby expanding her experimental sample and her opportunities for observation.

By implementing her method in the widest possible range of contexts, she accumulated the relevant evidence needed to support her broad claims about learning and development (Kramer, 1988; Foschi, 2012).

text.text: Her insistence on controlling the method, the training of teachers, and the construction of materials, which biographers have consistently read as rigidity or possessiveness, is on this reading the insistence of a scientist on the integrity of her protocol.

As she writes: "What I want now is a body of colleagues, research workers, who will examine what I have already done, apply my principles as far as I have gone, not in spirit of opposition or conviction, but as a matter of pure experiment" (Montessori, in Kramer, 1988: 262).

text.text: The progressive editions of the Metodo illustrate this dynamic clearly.

Trabalzini (Montessori, 2000; Trabalzini & Michener-Rutledge, 2023) identifies three main phaseshttps://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/Lio2 the first edition of 1909, the most scientific in spirit, opening with citations of Ernst Heinrich Weber, Gustav Fechner, and Wilhelm Wundt as representatives of experimental psychology, and containing extensive references to morphological research; the 1926 edition, modified to be acceptable to Catholic readers and blessed by Pope Benedict XV, which "dilutes references to the naturalistic-biological matrix, retouching or replacing the passages that might lead the reader to think she was advocating almost unconditional freedom" (Trabalzini & Michener-Rutledge, 2023) : 58); and the final edition of 1948/1950, renamed La scoperta del bambino [The Discovery of the Child] to reflect the accumulated results of decades of cross-cultural observation, in which she removed several of the religious elements, having recognised both that they were unnecessary and that they risked preventing children of different cultural and ethnic backgrounds from adopting the method.

text.text: Each modification expanded the potential audience and thus the experimental reach of the method, at the cost of its most technical scientific style.
What looks like the progressive abandonment of science is better understood as a trade-off between scientific communication and scientific practice.
This trade-off was consistently resolved in favour of practice, while it has been misread as evidence of her distance from sciencefoot_1.

The scientific character of Montessori's work was further obscured by the process of translation and international reception.
The most obvious instance is the fate of her first and most famous book.

Its original Italian title, Il metodo della pedagogia scientifica applicato all'educazione infantile nelle case dei bambini [The Method of Scientific Pedagogy Applied to Children's Education in the Children's Houses], retains the experimental nature of her methodology explicitly.
Its international title, The Montessori Method, strips all of this away, presenting the book as the proprietary method of a named individual rather than as a contribution to scientific pedagogy.
This is not a trivial difference.
It reframes the entire project: from an experimental investigation into cognitive development to a branded educational methodology.
The problem of translation extends beyond titles.

Montessori's Italian is technically loaded, although often outdated, in ways that her English translations consistently miss or misrepresent, with consequences that are directly relevant to reading her as a scientist interested in cognition.
This is particularly evident in La mente del bambino.

text.text: These translation losses are not incidental.
They systematically reduce the attempt of Montessori to offer a theoretically precise language, making her sound only as a practical educator, while downplaying her scientific coherent framework.

In fact, the terms that are lost or mistranslated (e.g., embodiment, active environmental sampling, constructing adaptation, psychical body) are precisely the terms that connect her work to contemporary cognitive science.

Mente Assorbente has a complex publication history.

It originated as a series of lectures delivered in English in India in 1949, first published as The Absorbent Mind by the Theosophical Publishing House in Adyar-Madras in the same year, and subsequently rewritten by Montessori in Italian and published in 1952.
The Italian 2023 Feltrinelli edition, which we cite as the primary text throughout this paper, is based on the 1952 Italian version.
The English translation we compare against is the 1988 Clio Press edition.

The relationship between the English lectures, the Italian rewriting, and the available English translation is itself a document of the translation problem: the "original" in this case is already a translation back from Italian of a text first delivered in English, making the theoretical precision of the Italian version all the more significant as evidence of Montessori's own considered formulations.

text.text: When the focus shifts from Italian to Anglophone literature, and from small local publishers to international peer-reviewed journals outside of the educational fields, the scientific components of Montessori's work disappear almost entirely from view.
The Anglophone reception was further shaped by a specific and influential misreading.

William Kilpatrick, student of John Dewey (i.e., one of the most influential figures in American progressive education) attended Montessori's classes in Italy and published a highly critical review of her method in 1914.

Kilpatrick read Montessori as scientifically old-fashioned: individualistic, focused on sensory training, insufficiently social, and grounded in a psychology that had already been superseded (Kilpatrick, 1914; Thayer-Bacon, 2012).

text.text: This reading, coming from within Dewey's research group, had a disproportionate influence on how Montessori was received in the academia in the United States and by extension in much of the Anglophone world (Gutek & Gutek, 2016).

text.text: It locked her into an educational frame from which she never fully escaped in international literature 14.
The third cause is structural: an academic environment that was deeply hostile to female scholars, particularly in scientific and technical fields.

She was among the first women to study medicine in Italy, attending at the cost of numerous special arrangements (e.g., dissecting cadavers alone rather than alongside male classmates) and only after having attended the faculty of Natural Sciences (Kramer, 1988: 35-38).

text.text: Her academic appointments -i.e., two short periods of "libera docenza" in anthropology, in 1904 at the Faculty of Natural Sciences and from 1906 to 1910 at the Pedagogical School of Rome, both obtained only through the intervention of Sergi -were precarious, unaffiliated, and paid by students directly.
No stable academic position followed.
The contradictions of Sergi's role are worth noting.
He supported Montessori's attempts to obtain academic positions and wrote letters of recommendation on her behalf, while simultaneously publishing on the scientific inferiority of women.

Se vi sono donne di genio [Whether there are Women of Genius] (https://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/hGBO) appeared precisely when Montessori was attending his classes and, under his suggestion, she was representing Italy at the International Congress for Women's Rights in Berlin (Kramer, 1988).

text.text: The contradiction is less surprising than it appears: Sergi considered Montessori an exceptional case while holding the general belief in female intellectual inferiority.
Despite his efforts on her behalf, she obtained nothing more than precarious appointments and never secured a permanent academic home.

text.text: His main objection, that is, that Montessori's method was too focused on sensory and perceptual training, for instance, are precisely the points on which developmental cognitive science has most decisively moved in Montessori's direction rather than Dewey's.

The emphasis on sensory and perceptual engagement as the foundation of abstract cognition, and on the material environment as a constitutive rather than merely contextual factor in development, dismissed by Kilpatrick as old-fashioned, are now central commitments of the field.

Her work developed instead through the movement that bore her name (schools, training programmes, international associations) which provided the experimental reach she needed but confirmed her image as an educator rather than a scientist, forcing her to appeal to a wider public through channels that the academic world did not recognise.
The gender dimension intersects with the style and reception problems in a specific way that Thayer-Bacon (2012) has identified.
Dewey, despite championing women's rights, consistently failed to cite the contributions of his female collaborators in his publications, contributing to their intellectual erasure.

Kilpatrick's critical review of Montessori, emerging from Dewey's research group, should be read in this context: it was not merely an intellectual disagreement but a gendered act of boundary-drawing that determined whose work counted as science and whose counted as practice.

The fact that Montessori was a European woman working in a continental tradition that American psychologists already considered old-fashioned (i.e., the German and French experimental and comparative psychology, the Italian biological anthropology, the comparative anatomy, ecology, and ethology that, all together, later gave rise to cognitive science) compounded the disadvantage at every level.
Together, these three causes produced a misreading that is historically overdetermined.
No single factor was decisive, and none has an intellectual basis.
The style shift was driven by financial necessity and experimental ambition, not by the abandonment of scientific rigour.
The translation losses were the product of dissemination urgency and commercial reframing, not of any absence of theoretical content in the original.
The gender and institutional exclusion reflected the structural conditions of early twentieth-century academia, not any deficiency in Montessori's scientific standing.
What got lost is the incorporation of a genuinely productive theoretical framework into the history of cognitive science and developmental psychology at the moment when that history was being made.
We examine this loss in the following section.

The three causes of misreading identified in Section 3 -the style shift, the translation losses, the gender and institutional exclusion -operated primarily at the level of reception: they determined how Montessori's work was read, classified, and positioned within the emerging scientific landscape (Whitescarver & Cossentino, 2008).

text.text: But the misreading had a further consequence: the theoretical framework Montessori had developed, an account of cognitive development as individual, material, and cultural simultaneously, was partially absorbed, stripped out its most important features, and then canonised in a form that made Montessori's contribution invisible.
Jean Piaget gives us an example of this.
A full comparison of Montessori's and Piaget's theories lies beyond the scope of this paper (but see: (Ültanır, 2012)).

text.text: Our aim is not to adjudicate between the two frameworks.
However, we note, in passing, that Montessori's account appears to us more coherent with the directions contemporary cognitive science has taken today, for reasons that will become apparent.

Our aim in this work is to show that the connections between Montessori's framework and contemporary cognitive science might have gone unnoticed in large part because of the misreading we have traced in the preceding sections.
The Piaget Author's Manuscript Submitted to History of Psychology case is the sharpest illustration of how that misreading operated at the level of the history of science itself.

Had Montessori been read also as a scientist rather than only as an educator, that is, had she been a man and held a stable academic position, or had her early Italian publications reached international audiences, the history of the sciences of the mind might have looked different today.

To be clear, the Piaget case is not a story of intellectual dishonesty but of historical contingency: how theoretical frameworks travel, get absorbed through proximity and exposure, and in the process both preserved and distorted.
The evidence for Piaget's sustained exposure to Montessori's work is substantial and has been underestimated in the literature.

text.text: The structural similarities between the two theories are unsurprising in this light: the constructivist emphasis on the child as active agent, the developmental trajectory from sensorimotor engagement to abstract thought, the constitutive role of the environment in cognitive formation.
Both thinkers also shared a biological formation that predisposed them toward a naturalistic, developmental account of mind.

There is reason to think, moreover, that Piaget was genuinely drawn to Montessori's concept of 'sensitive periods', which may have contributed more than has been acknowledged to what he would later formalise as genetic epistemology.

Montessori's theory of development could be considered an historical "elephant in the room" of Piaget's theory: present everywhere in its structure but not completely acknowledged, in a way reflecting the same gendered dynamics of intellectual erasure that Thayer-Bacon (2012) identified.

It also reflects the institutional asymmetry: Piaget was a professor at Geneva with a fully equipped research programme and international standing; Montessori was the founder of an educational movement, classified as an educator, and therefore not a scientific interlocutor.
In fact, Piaget did cite Montessori [e.g., (Piaget, 1970) https://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/SS2k, but the trajectory of his engagement is telling.

text.text: That he could recognise what she had accomplished while simultaneously refusing to engage with her as a thinker is perhaps the sharpest illustration of the gendered intellectual erasure that shaped the reception of Montessori work 15.
Piaget's genetic epistemology aligned with the constructivist core of Montessori's account and formalised it into a stage theory of remarkable precision and influence.

But the formalisation diverged from Montessori's framework in three respects, each concerning a feature central to her account: the continuity of development across individually variable sensitive periods, the constitutive role of the specific material environment, and the intelligence of perception and action from the earliest stages of development.
We address each in turn.
The first divergence concerns the relationship between continuity and individuality in development.
Montessori's piani di sviluppo [planes of development] are not stages in Piaget's sense.

They are defined by the sensitive periods during which each child constructs its own individual developmental trajectory, guided by its embodied capabilities and the activities it engages in within its material and cultural world.

The boundaries between planes are gradual and individual -"each level descends from the previous one and in turn prepares the next" (Tornar & Ahlquist, 2023 https://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/BLmY 67) -and the pace and character of development within each plane varies significantly across individuals and cultural contexts, making it the teacher's task to discern each child's developmental position.

text.text: Piaget's stages, by contrast, are discrete, universal, and largely context-independent: every child ought to pass through every stage in the same order, at roughly the same age, regardless of individual variation (Piaget, 1962).

text.text: This formalisation made the theory testable and generalisable, but at a cost: it abstracted away from precisely the individual variation and cultural embeddedness that Montessori's framework was designed to capture.

This tension is articulated at a deeper level in contemporary research. Bich and Skillings (Bich & Skillings, 2022) argue that stage-based accounts of development implicitly adopt what they call "adultocentrism": the improper fixation on the adult form as the true or proper form of the organism, which injects a forward-looking teleology into all developmental processes and reduces every prior stage to a merely preparatory condition.

text.text: Against this, they propose that development should be understood as the maintenance of organisational viability at each moment: there are no intermediate stages defined by their relation to some later achievement, only successive self-maintaining organisations, each with its own integrity.
Montessori's piani di sviluppo anticipate this position precisely.

text.text: What makes these dismissals particularly revealing is that they appear alongside passages in which Piaget accurately describes her theoretical contribution: "during its earliest stages the child learns more by action than through thought: suitable school equipment, serving to provide this action with raw material, lead toward knowledge more rapidly than either the best books or even language itself.

Thus the skillful observation of a psychiatric assistant of the mental mechanisms of backward children were the point of departure for a general method whose repercussions throughout the entire world have been incalculable" (Ibid.: 148).
Piaget here describes, with considerable precision, the embodied, material, action-based account of early cognitive development that is the theoretical core of Montessori's framework.
However, he attributes it to intuition and clinical observation rather than to theoretical and multidisciplinary insight.
What he cannot quite bring himself to recognise is that what he is describing is already a theory.

text.text: The second divergence concerns the role of the material environment.
Piaget recognised that the child constructs knowledge through action on objects, and that even early representations are grounded in action.

But he treated the environment as essentially interchangeable: any sufficiently rich physical setting would support normal cognitive development, and specific contexts had minimal influence on a developmental sequence that unfolds regardless (Babakr et al., 2019).

text.text: For Montessori, as we have shown in Section 2, these were the theoretical core.
This is not to claim a rigid one-to-one mapping between materials and cognitive outcomes.

Montessori's materials typically afford several forms of engagement at once, as when the map and geometry insets train geographical or geometrical understanding while simultaneously preparing the hand for holding a pen (A. Lillard, 2008; A. S. Lillard, 2016; Montessori, 2012 Montessori, , 2013)).

text.text: The third divergence is the separation of intelligence from action.

Piaget begins with the sensorimotor intelligence of the infant reachinghttps://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/tTEZ grasping, and manipulating (Piaget, 2008) , but his developmental sequence is structured as a progressive interiorisation and abstraction of action.

text.text: At the formal operational stage, intelligence is defined by its independence from reality content: by the capacity for hypothetical reasoning that holds "regardless of the intrinsic truth or falseness of the premises" (Ibid.: 42).
The child's body and the material world drop out of the definition of intelligence at precisely the moment it reaches its mature form.
Piaget's constructivism thus harbours a rationalist endpoint: the ideal cognitive agent is one who has successfully freed thought from its embodied, material origins.

That this constitutes a structural tension within Piaget's own framework, rather than an external misreading, is suggested by the fact that even sympathetic reconstructions of his theory acknowledged "the ever-growing divorce between action and cognition" as a live problem in the field (Lourenço & Machado, 1996) https://paperpile.com/c/7a2BJu/TzJM 158).

text.text: This integration is not the endpoint of a process that begins elsewhere, but the culmination of a developmental trajectory in which intelligence and action were never separated to begin with.

Already in the infant, Montessori insists, the activity of the senses is not passive reception but active engagement: the infant is "un cercatore attivo nell'ambiente" [an active seeker in the environment], and the impressions absorbed become "parte integrante della sua psiche" [integral part of its psyche] (Montessori, 2023: 150).

text.text: The continuity between the infant's sensory exploration and the mature child's concentrated, self-directed work is not a developmental achievement in Piaget's sense, and it does not require the transcendence of embodiment.
It is, instead, the progressive expression of what Montessori considered to be La mente del bambino: Mente assorbente [The Mind of the Child.
The Absorbent Mind] (Montessori, 2023): the child's distinctive capacity to take in, internalise, and be transformed by the cultural and material environment it inhabits.
This is an embodied, enactive account of infant cognition, from the first sensory impressions of infancy through to the fully integrated intelligence of the mature piano di sviluppo.

The three differences identified in the preceding section are precisely the points on which developmental cognitive science has most substantially revised the Piagetian framework in recent decades, arriving at positions that Montessori's work had already staked out.

Dynamical systems accounts have proposed that cognitive capacities emerge from the continuous interaction of the child's body, motor activity, and environment, rather than from the maturation of discrete internal structures.

Material engagement theory, as we discussed in Section 1, has argued that the specific material structure of the environment is not a contextual variable but a constitutive factor in cognition and that artefacts are not neutral props but active participants in cognitive processes that shape the abstract capacities through concrete interaction (Malafouris, 2013 (Malafouris, , 2019 (Malafouris, , 2020)).

text.text: That the recognition has been slow is itself a consequence of the misreading traced in this paper.

Montessori was classified as an educator, her work was read through a pedagogical lens, and the theoretical framework she had developed was encountered, where it was encountered at all, in a form that made its scientific content difficult to see.
The convergence is nonetheless real, and its documentation is the principal contribution this paper has attempted to make.

This paper has argued that Maria Montessori was a scientist of the developing mind whose work belongs in the history of cognitive science, as a coherent theoretical framework, grounded in a specific and traceable intellectual genealogy, that addresses the problems cognitive science is only now formalising with the precision they deserve.
Montessori did not call herself a cognitive scientist, and cognitive science did not exist in her lifetime.

However, she was pursuing, with rigour and originality, at least some of the problems and methods the discipline would later institutionalise, from a formation that was, in its interdisciplinary range and its commitment to integrating structure and function, brain and behaviour, individual and environment, more thoroughly proto-cognitive-scientific than the formation of many figures who are routinely included in the history of the field.
The misreading that has kept her out of that history, and the history of science in general, is not intellectually justified.

It is the product of three historically contingent processes: the transformation of her communicative style under financial and political pressure; the losses incurred in translation and international reception; and the structural exclusion she faced as a woman in a male-dominated academic environment.
None of them has any bearing on the theoretical content of her work.

Reading her correctly, through her untranslated early publications and the intellectual context of late nineteenth-century Rome, reveals a framework of remarkable coherence and contemporary relevance: an account of cognitive development in which individual variation, designed material environments, and cultural context are irreducible and simultaneous dimensions of a single developmental process.
What the recovery of Montessori's cognitive science offers is not merely a correction to the historical record, though it is that.
It is an invitation to read a rich and underexplored body of work, including the untranslated Italian sources on which this paper has drawn, with the theoretical seriousness it deserves.
The school, Montessori insisted, is a laboratory.
The laboratory has been open for over a century, and only a few seem to have noticed.

text.text: The gap between Montessori's public recognition and her institutional marginalisation is nowhere more vividly illustrated than at the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco in 1915, where a glass-walled Montessori demonstration classroom drew crowds of spectators, described by one newspaper as "as warm a coterie of fans as any home club with a winning streak ever drew inside a baseball grounds," and by another as "like tourists at an aquarium"(San Francisco Chronicle, in Sobe, 2004: 282).

text.text: The glass classroom is itself a revealing object: simultaneously a scientific demonstration (observation of children working freely in a prepared environment) and a public spectacle, watched by thousands who returned repeatedly over four months.

That same year, Montessori addressed the National Education Association (NEA) in Oakland, California, where she encapsulated her method in the declaration: "When you have solved the problem of controlling the attention of the child, you have solved the entire problem of education"(Montessori, 1915, in Sobe, 2004: 283).

The NEA address and the glass classroom together speak to a remarkable reach: Montessori was simultaneously drawing popular crowds, addressing the most prominent educational association in the United States, and being dismissed by academic psychologists as old-fashioned and insufficiently scientific.
That this could happen at the same moment is precisely the paradox this section attempts to explain.

text.text: The materials themselves reflect this absence of a fixed endpoint.

text.text: Montessori designed many of them to be encountered repeatedly across different ages and developmental stages, affording progressively more sophisticated understanding at each return.

A material calibrated to be interesting within a certain age range does not thereby cease to be interesting beyond it: the same object may become engaging again, or engaging for different reasons, as the child's developmental position changes.

The mathematical materials are exemplary here: the same concrete object that first affords basic quantity discrimination can later afford insight into more abstract numerical relations, depending on what the child or the adult brings to the encounter.
The material does not mark a stage to be passed and left behind but supports a continuous trajectory in which earlier engagements are revisited and deepened rather than superseded(Montessori, 2023).
